In a natural setting, light, especially morning light
synchronises the internal body clock to the earth’s 24-h
light–dark rotational cycle. Without the regular 24-h
light–dark cycle, the internal clock would be free-running.
‘‘Morning-type’’ humans have a free-running time shorter
than 24h, while ‘‘evening-type’’ humans have a free-
running time longer than 24h. The average for humans is
around 24h and 15–30min. The difference between an
individual’s own free-running time and the 24-h cycle
produces ever-greater day-to-day deviations in our body
temperature, cortisol and melatonin levels from those set
bytheenvironmentalclocktime(Czeisleretal.,1999).This
desynchronisation in the absence of the ‘‘normal’’ light–
dark rhythm would result in a wrong rhythm of alertness
and sleepiness, ultimately leading to alertness during the
dark hours and sleepiness during the bright hours. The
same symptoms, and for the same reason, that are in fact
associated with jet lag after travelling over several time
zones (Boulos et al., 1995). Rotating shift workers also
experience the same symptoms for a couple of days after
each shift change, again for the same reason (Akerstedt,
1985).
